pedagogy.summary: Children learn to recognise each UK coin (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2) and note (£5, £10, £20, £50) and to know its VALUE — crucially, that a coin's value is a matter of convention, not its physical size, colour, or the number of coins. The central hurdle is that value is invisible: a small silver 5p is worth more than a larger bronze 2p, and one £2 coin is worth more than a heap of pennies. Learned through handling real money and repeatedly asking 'what is it WORTH?', not 'how big / how many?'.
bestPractices: Handle real coins and notes; sort and name them by value, not by appearance
Ask 'what is this worth?' and 'which is worth more?', separating value from size, colour and number
Contrast a small high-value coin with a large low-value one (5p vs 2p; £1 vs 2p)
Order coins by value along a value line (1p to £2)
Introduce notes once coins are secure; say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies (avoid 'a hundred times bigger', which invites size confusion)
keyRepresentations: Coins ordered on a value line (1p to £2)
A 'worth' label held separate from the coin's appearance
commonMisconceptions: Judges value by physical size or colour (a 2p is bigger than a 5p, so 'worth more')
Thinks more coins means more money (a pile of pennies beats a single £2)
Confuses one penny and one pound
Doesn't recognise notes as money, or treats all notes as the same value

learn.summary: Young children (5-6) learn to recognise UK coins (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2) and notes (£5, £10, £20, £50) and to know each one's VALUE. The core hurdle is that value is invisible and set by convention, not by physical size, colour, or how many coins there are: a small silver 5p is worth more than a larger bronze 2p, and one £2 coin is worth more than a small heap of pennies (for example, ten 1p coins make only 10p). Activities centre on handling real money and repeatedly asking 'what is it WORTH?' rather than 'how big?' or 'how many?'.

activities.title: Till total: more coins is not always more money
feedback: If a child expects the heap of pennies to win 'because there are more', count the value of each set together: ten 1p = 10p versus one £2 = 200p, so fewer coins can be worth more.

If a child says the bigger 2p is worth more, ask 'what is it WORTH?' and point to the value shown on each coin (some designs show a number; others, such as the 2008–2022 shield designs, show the value only in words like 'TWO PENCE' and 'FIVE PENCE', so name the value for the child) — 5p is more than 2p, so the small 5p wins.
Reinforce by repeating the duel with different pairs (£1 vs 2p) so worth is separated from size and colour.
activities.rationale: Making the TOTAL VALUE visible and recomputing it as coins are added lets a child directly feel that value is independent of count and size, targeting the two central misconceptions (size/colour and more-coins-more-money). A running-total mat or till is one concrete way to make this mechanism visible; real coins counted together serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y2 Money documents pupils counting the NUMBER of coins rather than their value ('Tiny has counted the number of £2 coins, not their value') and introduces the term 'worth'.
learnerActions: Drop real coins (or coins onto a running-total mat/till) one at a time and watch the TOTAL VALUE build up.
Drop ten 1p coins into the till and read the total (10p); then drop a single £2 coin beside them and see the total leap far higher than the whole heap of pennies.
Say in your own words why one coin can be worth more than many coins.
Run a 'which is worth more?' duel: put a big bronze 2p against a small silver 5p, predict which wins, then reveal/count the values to check.
activities.intendedInsight: A set's worth is its total VALUE, not the number of coins or their size; one high-value coin can outweigh many low-value coins, and the smaller coin can be worth more.

activities.title: Order coins on a value line
feedback: If a child orders by size, point to the printed value and re-place the coin by what it is WORTH.
Praise reasoning that cites the number/value on the coin rather than its appearance.
activities.rationale: Ordering by value along a line gives a durable mental sequence and repeatedly surfaces the small-coin-worth-more discriminator. Dragging coins onto a value line by worth (not size) is one concrete interactive form; a physical sorting mat and real coins work equally well.
learnerActions: Handle real coins and sort them, naming each by its value.
Place each coin in order from least worth to most worth along a value line running 1p to £2 (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2).
Notice where a physically small coin (5p) sits ahead of a physically bigger coin (2p) on the line.
Answer 'which is worth more?' for pairs you place, giving the value as your reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Coins have a fixed order BY VALUE that does not follow their physical size or colour; a 5p comes after a 2p even though it is smaller.

activities.title: Recognise and compare coins and notes
feedback: If a child confuses one penny and one pound, lay a real 1p and £1 side by side, name each, and say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies.
If a child treats all notes as the same, compare the printed values and ask which note is worth more.
When a child reads the number on a coin to decide, confirm that the number tells us what it is worth.
activities.rationale: Recognition is the stated curriculum objective and benefits from naming, value-recall and worth comparisons. A tap-to-reveal coin-and-note chart or lift-the-flap comparison is one supportive format; real coins and notes handled directly are the primary medium. Saying 'worth a hundred pennies' rather than 'a hundred times bigger' avoids inviting size confusion, per NCETM guidance.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'recognise and know the value of different denominations of coins and notes'.

NCETM guidance states 'Some children may confuse one pence and one pound' and advises 'It is helpful to avoid saying that one pound is one hundred times bigger than one penny as children may think this refer to the coin size rather than the value' — grounding the coin-value-independent-of-physical-size misconception.
learnerActions: Look at each coin and note and name it and say its value.
Reveal or state a comparison fact for each: 'is this worth more than, less than, or the same as a 10p?'
Introduce notes once coins are secure: name £5, £10, £20, £50 and say which is worth more.
Say that a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies (not 'a hundred times bigger').
activities.intendedInsight: Every coin and note can be recognised and matched to a known value, and notes are money too — different notes have different values.

activities.title: Shopkeeper: hand over coins by value
feedback: If a child hands over a coin chosen by size, ask them to read its value and pick again by worth.
Encourage answers that name the value rather than describe the colour or size.
activities.rationale: A role-play shopkeeper elicits recognition and value selection through talk and action and adds a purposeful context. This is a supporting activity: it is strongest when the child also physically handles and hands over real coins, so recognition is shown by doing, not only by speaking.
learnerActions: Play a shop where a shopkeeper asks you to hand over a coin by its value ('give me the one worth 5p', 'give me something worth more than a 10p').
Explain out loud why the coin you chose is worth what the shopkeeper asked.
Swap roles so you ask for coins by value too.
activities.intendedInsight: You can identify and select coins by their worth, using value rather than appearance to respond.

constraints: Use real coins and notes as the primary medium; interactive charts, tills and value lines are scaffolds that support, not replace, handling money.
Always ask 'what is it WORTH?' rather than 'how big?' or 'how many?', so value is held apart from size, colour and number.
Introduce notes only once coin recognition and value are secure.
Say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies; avoid 'a hundred times bigger', which invites size confusion.

A recognition matching/ordering/'which is worth more' task can check and reinforce value knowledge, but on its own it elicits selection rather than the child independently handling, totalling and explaining worth; pair it with hands-on comparison.
The shopkeeper talk activity supports recognition but should include physically handing over coins, not only naming them aloud.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (White Rose Y2 Money) was marked verified:false in the original row; treat its 'counting number not value' example and the term 'worth' as unconfirmed, including where it is used as a sourceClaim on the till activity.

The original row claimed '3D adds nothing' for coin value. Coin value is indeed not a spatial concept, but this is a scoped observation, not an established universal law; a 3D/physical model could still support handling. Rephrased as medium guidance rather than a prohibition.

The original framed the till/value-line as the single format where the insight 'lands'. Retained as one concrete mechanism, not as the only way to teach it; counting real coins together serves the same purpose.

The Year 1 curriculum claim was left attached only to the recognition activity, where it directly matches the objective; it was removed from the value-line ordering activity's sourceClaims because it supports the general objective, not that specific method.

The assessment's ten-1p-vs-50p comparison was adapted to ten-1p-vs-£2 in the till activity (ten 1p = 10p vs one £2 = 200p); this is internally consistent and preserves the 'fewer coins can be worth more' principle, but differs from the original assessment numbers, which remain valid.

assess.poeTask: Put a heap of ten 1p coins next to a single 50p. Ask the child to PREDICT which is more money and, crucially, WHY, before anyone counts. Then count the value of the heap together (10p) against the 50p. A child who predicted the heap 'because there are more' meets the moment where fewer coins are worth more.
probeDeeper: 'This 5p is smaller than the 2p — so how can it be worth more?' (size vs value)
'You have more coins, but is it more money? Let's count what each pile is worth.'
'What does the number on the coin tell us?'
'If I gave you one £2 coin or five 20p coins, would you have the same amount? Which would you rather have?' (same value, different count)
assess.correctAnswer: Says the 5p is worth more than the 2p BECAUSE 5 is more than 2 (its value, not its size); says the single 50p is more money than ten pennies (50 > 10) despite fewer coins; says £2 > 50p and £10 > £5 by their values.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges value by physical size or colour — a bigger coin is 'worth more' (the 2p is bigger than the 5p)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly — compare the printed values; handle a small high-value coin against a big low-value one repeatedly, always asking 'what does it say it is WORTH?'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the reason tier says the 2p is worth more 'because it is bigger'

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks more coins means more money — a pile of pennies beats a single higher-value coin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by counting the VALUE of each set (ten 1p = 10p vs 50p); show that one coin can be worth more than many.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ten 1p coins, because there are more of them
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the ten 1p coins over the 50p 'because there are more'

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses one penny and one pound
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two explicitly with real coins; say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies rather than 'a hundred times bigger', which invites the size confusion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats a 1p and a £1 as the same, or says £1 is 'one'

responseLevels.gap: Names some coins but judges 'worth more' by size, colour or number of coins; confuses penny and pound.
responseLevels.full: Recognises all coins and notes and compares them by VALUE, knowing value is independent of size, colour and number of coins (a small 5p beats a 2p; one 50p beats ten pennies; £2 > 50p).
responseLevels.partial: Recognises and names the coins/notes and reads their numbers, but is still caught when the smaller coin is worth more or a pile of small coins is set against one large-value coin.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the value, THEN the reason: (1) Show a 5p and a 2p: 'Which coin is worth more?' then 'How do you know?' (2) Show ten 1p coins beside one 50p: 'Which is more money?' then 'Why?' (3) 'Which is worth more, a £2 coin or a 50p coin? How do you know?' and 'Point to the £5 note and the £10 note — which is worth more?' Listen to the REASON: a correct child cites the printed value; an incorrect one cites size, colour or how many.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 5p-vs-2p item is the hinge: the smaller coin is worth more, so a child reasoning by size gives the wrong answer while a child reasoning by value gives the right one — hard to get right for the wrong reason. The ten-pennies-vs-50p item catches 'more coins = more money'.
